title: Justice Dept. Seeks Separate Alaska Ballots Ranking Dan J. Sullivan in Senate Race, NBC Reports
body:
A federal judge in Alaska has been asked by the Justice Department to issue an emergency order that would require election officials to separate every ballot that lists Senate hopeful Dan J. Sullivan in a “rank‑choice” column, a move the administration says is needed to prevent “voter confusion.” The request, filed late Friday, seeks a directive by Monday that would compel the state’s election office to isolate those ballots from the rest of the tabulation process, a step that could delay the final count in a race that has already drawn national attention.

The filing argues that the presence of a separate “rank‑choice” column on Alaska’s new voting system—introduced for the first time in the 2022 midterms—creates ambiguity for voters who may not understand how to correctly rank candidates. The Justice Department’s brief, however, does not explain precisely how physically separating the ballots would clarify voter intent, nor does it provide evidence that the current counting method leads to misinterpretation. Critics say the request appears more political than procedural, pointing out that Sullivan, a former state legislator and former deputy attorney general, is the only major candidate whose name appears in the rank‑choice field, raising questions about the true motive behind the filing.

Alaska’s adoption of a hybrid voting system—combining a traditional first‑place vote with a separate rank‑choice option—was intended to give voters more flexibility while preserving the familiar “first‑past‑the‑post” outcome. Under the system, a voter can either select a single candidate for the Senate seat or rank multiple candidates in order of preference. Election officials have stated that the software automatically reconciles the two columns, ensuring that a ballot is counted only once, according to the voter’s expressed choice. The Justice Department’s demand to physically segregate ballots would require election staff to manually sort and recount, a process that could introduce human error and extend the certification timeline.

Legal scholars note that the request may run afoul of established election law principles, particularly the “one‑person, one‑vote” doctrine and the federal requirement that states provide clear, uniform voting procedures. “The courts have repeatedly emphasized that any change to ballot handling must be narrowly tailored and supported by concrete evidence of a problem,” said Professor Emily Ramirez, a voting‑rights expert at the University of Washington. “A blanket order to separate ballots without showing how the current method actually confuses voters is unlikely to meet the stringent standards for injunctive relief.”

The move also arrives amid a broader national debate over the integrity of rank‑choice voting, which has been adopted in several states and municipalities as an alternative to the traditional plurality system. Proponents argue that it reduces the spoiler effect and encourages more civil campaigning, while opponents claim it adds complexity and opens the door to legal challenges. The Alaska race, featuring incumbent Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski, former Republican Dan J. Sullivan, and several Democratic challengers, is seen as a bellwether for how the method will be perceived in future elections.

If the judge grants the Justice Department’s request, Alaska’s election officials will have only a few days to implement a new counting protocol, potentially postponing the certification of results that are expected in early December. The decision could also set a precedent for other states using rank‑choice voting, prompting similar challenges from parties that feel disadvantaged by the system. Conversely, a denial would reinforce the current process and signal that the courts are unwilling to intervene without clear, demonstrable harm.

As the deadline approaches, both sides are preparing for a legal showdown that could reshape Alaska’s electoral landscape. Regardless of the outcome, the case underscores the growing tension between innovative voting mechanisms and the entrenched legal frameworks that govern American elections. Observers will be watching closely to see whether the judiciary will prioritize procedural consistency or accommodate the political pressures that have brought this unprecedented request to the courtroom.
